Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Ground forces shell Ile de Cézembre with artillery, while Dinard is approached by land; on 7 August, the 121st Infantry under Colonel Jeter crosses the Rance to destroy the Dinard garrison, dispatches a force to take Dinan surrender, and advances north but encounters heavy artillery fire.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_52: Though ground forces alone could only shell the Ile de Cézembre with artillery, Dinard was approachable by land. On 7 August, while the 83d Division was launching its attack on St. Malo, the 181st Infantry (Col. John R. Jeter) had crossed the Rance to destroy the Dinard garrison.<sup>[37](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn21.html#fn37)</sup> Colonel Jeter dispatched a small force to take the surrender of the enemy force at Dinan, which had promised the FFI to capitulate to the Americans. Turning north from Dinan, the main body of the 121st Infantry soon came under heavy artillery fire.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: The 121st Infantry discovers heavily fortified roads to Dinard with roadblocks, pillboxes, wire, mine fields, and German automatic weapons; advance is slow, harassed by German fire.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_53: The 121st Infantry quickly discovered that every usable road to Dinard was barred by roadblocks of concrete, rock, felled trees, and barbed wire, each covered by camouflaged strongpoints manned by from twenty to eighty men armed with a high proportion of automatic weapons. The Germans also had constructed underground pillboxes and iron rail fences, strung double-apron barbed wire and concertina entanglements, and laid extensive mine fields. The pillboxes seemed unaffected by American artillery fire. German machine gun, small arms, mortar, and artillery fire harassed every American attempt to blast passageways through the other obstacles.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: On afternoon of 8 August, the 3d Battalion of 121st Infantry enters Pleurtuit, reduces pillboxes, but is isolated by German tanks and infantry re-establishing a roadblock.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_54: The 121st Infantry's advance was painfully slow. On the afternoon of 8 August, the 3d Battalion entered the village of Pleurtuit, less than four miles from Dinard. In the process it had reduced three pillboxes by close-in engineer and infantry action. As the troops moved into the village, several German tanks came in from the flanks and cut behind the battalion. Re-establishing a previously destroyed roadblock, German infantrymen isolated the unit.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Despite support, the 121st Infantry cannot break through to the isolated 3d Battalion; tragic incidents with artillery planes crashing while supporting the unit.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_55: Despite the support of strong artillery, mortar, and tank destroyer fire, the rest of the 121st Infantry could not break through to the battalion. Discouragement and tragedy marked the efforts. Two artillery planes, after successfully dropping blood plasma to the 3d Battalion, locked wings and crashed, their pilots and observers killed. A third plane was shot down by enemy fire. Two other planes flying observation missions in support of the isolated unit collided and crashed.<sup>[38](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn21.html#fn38)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Isolation of 3d Battalion confirms poor performance of 121st Infantry; on 9 August, after St. Joseph's Hill falls, General Macon reorganizes to prioritize Dinard reduction for multiple strategic purposes.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_56: The isolation of the 121st Infantry's 3d Battalion confirmed General Macon's impression that in general the regiment's performance west of the Rance had been far from brilliant, but only on 9 August, when St. Joseph's Hill fell, was General Macon able to turn full attention to the situation. When the capitulation of St. Joseph's Hill enabled the 83d Division to occupy St. Servan and Paramé, Macon decided to reorganize his forces, reshape the battle, and give priority to the reduction of Dinard.
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_57: Eliminating the Dinard garrison, a task General Macon judged to be relatively easy, would serve four purposes: it would stop part of the effective artillery fire that came from across the Rance; it would block the possibility that German troops might escape from the St. Malo fortress westward toward Brest; it would release the isolated battalion of the 121st Infantry; and it would make possible the return of the 121st to its parent organization for possible participation in a strong attack against Brest, an operation then under discussion.

Sub-Event-Images: Beach at Dinard, showing underwater obstacles planted by the Germans to prevent amphibious landings.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: General Macon reshuffles forces, replaces 331st with 330th in Paramé, moves 331st across Rance to reinforce 121st, and takes personal command of Dinard operation.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_58: To help the 121st Infantry take Dinard, General Macon first reshuffled his organic forces by replacing the 331st Infantry in the Paramé sector with the 330th and moving the 331st across the Rance to reinforce the 121st. Finally, he took personal command of the Dinard operation.<sup>[39](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn21.html#fn39)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: On 11 August, coordinated attack on Dinard begins but advance is slow, with evening counterattack repulsed; General Macon reports stronger resistance than anticipated; defense led by Colonel Bacherer with remnants of 77th Division, who defies surrender ultimatum.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_59: On 11 August, when General Macon got a co-ordinated attack on Dinard under way, physical contact with the 3d Battalion, 121st Infantry, still had not been established. The advance through the strongly fortified and stubbornly defended area continued painfully slow. The climax of a discouraging day came in the evening when a counterattack was repulsed with difficulty. "I want Monarch 6 [General Middleton] to know," a somewhat chastened General Macon radioed to the corps headquarters, "thatthe resistance we are meeting south of Dinard is more determined than I anticipated."<sup>[40](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn21.html#fn40)</sup>
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_60: The defense of Dinard was in the capable hands of Colonel Bacherer, who commanded a kampfgruppe composed in the main of remnants of the *77th Division,* veterans of earlier fighting in the Cotentin. Creating their own field expedients to augment the existing fortifications of the Dinard portion of the St. Malo fortress, the men fought ably. To a surrender ultimatum from General Macon, Bacherer replied defiantly: "Every house must become a fortress, every stone a hiding place, and for every stone we shall fight."<sup>[41](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn21.html#fn41)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Despite strong defense, on afternoon of 12 August, 331st Infantry breaks through around Pleurtuit, destroys bunkers and guns, takes prisoners, and makes contact with isolated 3d Battalion of 121st.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_61: Despite the excellence of the German positions and the will to resist, the Germans could not indefinitely withstand the pressure of two regiments plus the increasing power of a growing number of corps artillery battalions in support. On the afternoon of 12 August, the 331st Infantry broke through the German line around Pleurtuit. After destroying five bunkers by demolition and assault, knocking out an 88-mm. gun and several vehicles, and taking more than a hundred prisoners, the regiment at last made contact with the isolated battalion of the 121st.<sup>[42](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn21.html#fn42)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: During three days of isolation, 3d Battalion retains integrity against counterattacks with relatively low losses; heroic act by Pvt. Francis A. Gardner on 9 August, using bazooka to disable German tank and kill crew.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_62: Through three days of isolation, the battalion had retained its integrity in the face of several counterattacks launched with artillery support. Surprisingly, losses were not so high as had been feared--31 killed, 106 wounded, and 16 missing. The kind of courage that had sustained the battalion was exemplified by a heroic act on 9 August, not long after the force was isolated. No sooner had an artillery shell struck the battalion command post, killing the operations and motor officers and seriously wounding the operations sergeant and a radio operator, than a German tank appeared five hundred yards away. Opening fire, the tankers killed several men. For a moment it appeared that the battalion headquarters might be annihilated. Taking matters into his own hands, Pvt. Francis A. Gardner of the Headquarters Company ran toward the tank with a bazooka. Though his first rocket missed, a 57-mm. antitank gun firing at the same time immobilized the tank by a hit on the treads. As the German crew started to abandon the disabled tank, Gardner fired a second time, striking the turret and killing the crew.<sup>[43](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn21.html#fn43)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: With Pleurtuit secured, regiments continue attack on 13 August, reducing pillboxes; by afternoon of 14 August, enter Dinard and suburbs; operation completes on 15 August, clearing Dinard, St. Lunaire, St. Briac-sur-Mer, capturing Bacherer's headquarters and nearly 4,000 prisoners including Bacherer.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_63: With Pleurtuit in hand, the two regiments continued their attack on 13 August, slowly and systematically reducing individual pillboxes. By the afternoon of 14 August both regiments had entered Dinard and its suburbs. The operation was completed on the following day with the clearing of Dinard and the nearby villages of St. Lunaire and St. Briac-sur-Mer. Bacherer's headquarters, located in a small fort equipped with running water, air conditioning, food, and facilities to withstand siege, was captured. Surrender of the Dinard garrison added almost four thousand prisoners, including Bacherer, to the Allied bag.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: General Middleton remarks on 121st Infantry's performance; 83d Division chief of staff explains the slow progress and sudden breaks; notes that one regiment was insufficient west of the Rance, but two succeeded.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_64: When General Middleton remarked that the 121st Infantry didn't appear to have done much, the 83d Division chief of staff explained, "It is hard to tell what they have been up against. Sometimes those things go very slow for a while then all of a sudden they break. . . ."<sup>[44](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn21.html#fn44)</sup> The fact was that one regiment had not been enough west of the Rance but two had been able to do the job.
